items.stem: Why rely on a verified Stripe webhook rather than the client redirect to confirm a subscription?

options.text: The client redirect can be faked or lost; the signed webhook is authoritative
options.rationale: Correct: server-side verified webhooks are the reliable source of truth.

options.text: The redirect is encrypted end to end
options.rationale: The redirect is not a trustworthy confirmation of payment state.

options.text: Webhooks are slower so they are ignored
options.rationale: Webhooks are the authoritative event, not something to ignore.
Client state can be tampered with or interrupted.

items.explanation: Correct: server-side verified webhooks are the reliable source of truth.

items.stem: Which TWO practices protect a Stripe integration? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Verify the webhook signature before acting on the event
options.rationale: Correct: signature verification rejects forged events.

options.text: Keep the secret key on the server only
options.rationale: Correct: a secret key in client code is exposed to users.

options.text: Put the secret key in client-side JavaScript
options.rationale: Client code is fully visible to users.

options.text: Act on unverified webhook payloads immediately

items.explanation: Correct: signature verification rejects forged events.

items.stem: Why exercise failed-payment scenarios in Stripe test mode before launch?

options.text: Because dunning and recovery are part of the real subscription lifecycle
options.rationale: Correct: failed payments are common and must be handled, not assumed away.

options.text: Because test mode charges real cards
options.rationale: Test mode does not charge real cards.

options.text: Because failed payments never happen in production
options.rationale: Failed payments are routine in production.

options.text: Because it removes the need for webhooks
options.rationale: Webhooks are still needed to track payment state.

items.explanation: Correct: failed payments are common and must be handled, not assumed away.
